title: 6 Best Fitbit Models for Beginners, Athletes, and Kids (2026)
summary: The fitness trackers I’d recommend to beginners, athletes, and kids.
full_text:
It’s been five years since Google officially acquired Fitbit for a reported $2.1 billion, grabbing hardware and software teams that also absorbed assets from Pebble, which Fitbit itself acquired in 2016. So, how have things changed? Well, for starters, Fitbit is now Google Fitbit. It’s not the most imaginative of name changes, and it hasn't stuck in consumers’ minds, but the good news is that Fitbit devices remain some of the most user-friendly and welcoming fitness trackers available. This is especially true if you're just starting, or reigniting, your fitness journey.
Fitbit’s dominance has waned slightly in the face of countless alternatives, but its affordable approach, user-friendly interface, and great styling make it one of the best wearable fitness brands. If you’re looking for a reliable step-counting, sleep-tracking monitor, you’re in for a treat—and thanks to Google’s stewardship, you can now even find a smartwatch with features to rival the competition. Here are my picks of the best Fitbit trackers, whatever your wearable needs are.
For more wearable recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Fitness Trackers, Best Smart Rings, and Best Garmin Watches.
Updated July 2026: I've added the Google Fitbit Air and incorporated pros and cons to all of our recommendations. Product information, links, and prices were also updated.
Featured in This Guide
Best Fitbit Overall
If you don't need another screen competing for your attention, the Google Fitbit Air is the one I'd recommend to most people. At just 12 grams, it's the lightest Fitbit—you'll forget you're wearing it—yet it quietly tracks everything that matters: heart rate, sleep, daily activity, skin temperature variations, and menstrual health (to name a few). And instead of constantly checking stats on your wrist, you'll find all insights in the Google Health app, where your data is presented in an easy-to-understand format.
The Air nails the basics. Battery life stretches to about a week, and a five-minute top-up gets you roughly a day's worth of wear. Automatic workout detection can occasionally mistake one activity for another, and some of the AI guidance can feel generic, but those are minor trade-offs for a wearable that's comfortable enough to wear all day and night. Its $100 price also makes it one of the most affordable ways to get comprehensive health tracking. The biggest downside of the Air is also its biggest strength; there's no screen, so if you prefer having a display, go with the Fitbit Charge 6. But for most people, the Fitbit Air strikes the best balance of price, comfort, and everyday health tracking.
Best Fitbit for Beginners
Launched in 2023, the Charge 6 remains the best fitness tracker for beginners. It's the same slim build as its predecessor (the Fitbit Charge 5), maintaining the bright AMOLED touchscreen, with an optional always-on display, and fortunately bringing back the physical side button. It monitors your heart rate, blood oxygen, and skin temperature, and it offers ECG and electrodermal activity scans to measure irregular heart rhythms and stress level insights. The largest upgrade on the functionality front is the new ability to connect Fitbit's heart rate sensor to particular gym equipment like the NordicTrack treadmill or Peloton bike. In testing, its heart rate sensors held up well against the Oura ring. Battery life is also fantastic, with up to a week per charge.
The built-in GPS support doesn't rival dedicated sports watches for accuracy, but it's useful enough for outdoor activities. Plus, unlike those wearables, Fitbit dishes out detailed sleep data that is both insightful and actionable. Google’s presence has increased on the Charge with the useful additions of Google Maps and Google Wallet. You get all of this and more for less than the cost of Fitbit's smartwatches.
Most Affordable Fitbit (With Display)
Along with its budget price, the Inspire 3 also offers the longest battery life of the Fitbit lineup. A full charge will last you up to 10 days, depending on how much you use it. It is pretty similar to the Charge 6, except that it lacks a built-in GPS, and it only features 20 exercise modes (as opposed to Charge 6's 40 modes, which I found to be excessive anyway). You also miss out on some of the other premium features, such as Bluetooth compatibility with certain gym equipment, the EDA Scan app for stress management, and NFC technology. If none of those qualities matter to you, I would opt for the Inspire 3, which is just as accurate as the Charge 6.
Best Fitbit for Kids
The first Fitbit Ace landed in 2018, offering kids ages 8 and above the ability to track their steps and sleep and to be in constant pursuit of virtual badges. The Fitbit Ace LTE ditches the fitness band form for a smartwatch one, instantly giving it more grown-up kids appeal. The Ace LTE is built for ages 7 to 14 and comes with a design perhaps best described as a more child-friendly Versa. There’s a sizable OLED screen with Gorilla Glass 3 to fend off scratches, and unlike the first Ace, it can be submerged in water up to 50 meters deep.
There are some familiar fitness tracker sensors in place, including an optical heart rate monitor and motion sensors to track movement, though Fitbit has ditched the sleep-tracking support that was available on the original Ace. It has LTE connectivity so parents and children can make calls to each other, and it also taps into Google Maps to give it location-tracking smarts. Payments are on the way for the watch, too.
There are also games to play, including a very Fitbit take on a Tamagotchi that’s sure to appeal. There is the matter of a $10 per month subscription fee to get the complete Ace experience; it isn’t a cheap kids’ smartwatch either. But it’s easy to use, and it gets the balance of fun and fitness just right to make it a good fit for kids. —Michael Sawh
Best Fitbit Smartwatch
Now that the Google Pixel Watch 4 actually exists, the fate of Fitbit’s own smartwatches feels up in the air. But if the idea of owning a Pixel Watch doesn’t appeal and you’re interested in a more Fitbit-centric experience with better battery life, the Versa 4 is the one to go for. You get a smartwatch with a gently curved design; it’s almost identical to the original Versa, but with the welcome return of a physical button. There’s a large, vibrant, 1.5-inch AMOLED display touchscreen and a battery performance that can really stretch over the promised six days if you don’t leave the screen on 24/7.
As for sports, the Versa 4 is designed with a built-in GPS to track outdoor runs and rides and motion sensors to track indoor swims, though not with sports-watch-rivaling accuracy. Fitbit’s PurePulse heart rate sensor is a better fit for day-to-day heart rate stats than it is for a CrossFit class. And third-party app support has been replaced by native Google apps, like Maps, with Google Assistant joining Amazon’s Alexa. As a device that lets you check your phone notifications, keep an eye on step counts and sleep, and forget about constantly charging it, the Versa 4 has plenty to like. —Michael Sawh
Best Fitbit for Health Tracking
The Fitbit Sense 2 was meant to attract the kind of people who were looking at the Apple Watch. It's designed with an electrocardiogram (ECG) sensor that’s been approved in the US to help wearers detect potential signs of atrial fibrillation. A skin temperature sensor can monitor temperature changes during the night to spot any trends, and a SpO2 sensor goes to work when you’re sleeping to detect breathing disturbances. While it’s not a regulatory-approved feature, it can detect potential warning signs of a sleep disorder, like sleep apnea.
An electrical cEDA sensor captures on-the-spot and continuous measurements of galvanic skin response that Fitbit uses as a marker of stress. Fitbit needs to work on delivering information on potential stressors in a useful way, but it’s a start. The Sense 2 also grabs all of the cheaper Versa’

title: States Want ICE Agents to Show Their Faces. The Trump Administration Is Blocking Them
summary: Federal lawyers say anti-mask laws would endanger immigration agents, citing an ICE face-recognition art project that doesn’t actually work.
full_text:
The Trump administration has sued at least five states and the city of Philadelphia over laws that supporters say would hold law enforcement—including Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers—accountable for misconduct on the job. The specifics of the laws vary, but the Trump administration takes particular issue with the fact that the laws would prohibit ICE officers from wearing masks during immigration raids, and require them to wear some sort of individual identifier.
Having to show their faces, lawyers for the Trump administration argue, would put ICE officers in danger.
In complaints filed against New York, Virginia, Connecticut, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, attorneys for the federal government claim that people take photos of ICE officers to “run them through facial recognition applications that search social media and doxing sites,” specifically calling out an art project called ICESpy. (California was subject to a similar lawsuit months before the other states, but the DOJ did not mention ICESpy in that complaint.)
There's just one problem, according to ICESpy’s creator, artist Kyle McDonald: the art project's face-recognition software cannot recognize most, if any, ICE agents currently in the field.
ICESpy is based on photos, job titles, and names of people who self-identified as ICE nearly a decade ago on LinkedIn. WIRED viewed a version of the list, which had just over 700 entries, and found that the most common title was “assistant chief counsel,” and many of the people appeared to have executive, administrative, or legal roles. Only 39 people on it had “deportation officer” in their title, and an additional 27 had related titles such as “enforcement and removal assistant” or “immigration enforcement agent.”
Many deportation officers joined the agency well after the data was collected. In January, ICE announced that it had more than doubled its number of agents and officers in just a few months, from 10,000 to 22,000. None of those additional people would be in the database, unless they had another job with ICE in 2018 (and posted about it online).
“They make this claim that people are using this site and others to search for family members. They offer no evidence of this in the filing,” McDonald tells WIRED. “The idea that someone could use a site like ICESpy and find an active ICE deportation officer in 2026 is absurd.”
ICE did not respond to a request for comment.
Data issues aside, ICESpy is not popular. WIRED reviewed activity logs for ICESpy between June 30 and July 6, which showed there were only 84 page views that week—a remarkably small number, even for a niche art project website. Only two face-match attempts were made, and the results of both were so bad that McDonald says they could not possibly be a match of anyone in his dataset of 2018 LinkedIn users.
“Like, I'm sure people were playing with it at some point?? But it is not an active threat to ANYBODY Imao,” McDonald says in a text message.
Attorneys for the federal government also blame another site, ICE List, for aiding people interested in "doxing" ICE agents. ICE List describes itself as an accountability initiative, and keeps track of people involved with ICE and other agencies involved in deportation efforts, along with vehicles used on the job and incidents that occur during enforcement actions.
Individual agent pages on ICE List typically include the person’s name and general information about what their job title is, the field office they are associated with, and any incidents they might have been involved in along with links to public sources that corroborate the claims on the page. When WIRED analyzed the site in January, we found that it too relied mostly on data that self-described ICE employees had posted on LinkedIn. It also doesn't have any sort of public-facing way for visitors to try to computationally analyze photos, though some agent pages include headshots.
Dominick Skinner, ICE List’s maintainer, says the site has a small, dedicated group of people who try to use face recognition, but their success with the technology so far has been “overblown,” and the site mostly relies on manual research.
“I wish we had a tool good enough to take away the work 😂” Skinner tells WIRED via text message.
The group of ICE List users was recently credited for identifying David Brouillette, the ICE agent and former Army veteran who allegedly shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian living in Maine. In that case, the website put out a request for information from people in Bangor, Maine, and Skinner says two people close to Brouillette came forward. Brouillette’s ex-wife later told the Portland Press Herald that she had previously reported concerns about Brouillette’s mental health to his superiors in the US military. Brouillette did not respond to a request for comment.
Skinner says that ICE List doesn’t fit the traditional definition of doxing—it does not post agents’ home addresses or that of their family—and that data broker sites post far more intimate information about agents but don’t face the same level of scrutiny. Older guidance from the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, advises people to request to remove their personal data from such sites.
It’s unclear how many ICE agents have actually been identified because of ICESpy or ICE List. The Department of Justice, which is litigating the cases, did not put specific numbers in its complaints.
DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels says that “individuals have used facial recognition and doxxing tools to identify and harass federal law enforcement officers, and these sites frequently change domains, shut down, and reappear under new names.”
Pels did not respond to WIRED’s request for a concrete example of a protester using ICESpy to identify an ICE agent.
Meanwhile, state lawmakers say their laws requiring ICE agents to identify themselves are trying to address very real issues around democracy and justice, and the federal government should prioritize other work that’s within its remit.
“Instead of challenging these reasonable restrictions, the Department of Justice should seek accountability for the actions of poorly trained ICE agents, release the Epstein files, and investigate the Trump organization’s unprecedented corruption,” says Virginia state senator Saddam Salim, where the federal government successfully won an injunction pausing SB 352, the state’s new law that prohibits law enforcement in the state from wearing masks, among other restrictions.
ICE officers weren’t wearing congressionally mandated body cameras when they fatally shot two people in Maine and Texas this month, making it more difficult to investigate what happened. Federal officials refused to produce evidence to Minnesota investigators related to the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti for nearly half a year until they were compelled by the courts. WIRED recently reported that ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility, an internal watchdog that investigates employee misconduct, is busy looking into civilians who post criticism online about the federal government and its immigration policies.
“States have a right and an ability to be able to react and respond to what we see as unconstitutional behavior by our federal government,” says Bob Duff, a Connecticut state senator who worked on a law for his state that is now being challenged. “And we have a right and responsibility to protect our own residents in the state.”

title: A Teen Reporter Searched for His Community in the Epstein Files. Adults Freaked Out
summary: An Instagram post turned one California student newspaper into a free-speech flash point. The students say they were just doing their homework.
full_text:
Ben Mueller’s assignment for his journalism class was to tell a news story—any news story—in the form of an extended Instagram slideshow. So when the high school senior got home on the afternoon of February 10, 2026, he grabbed a snack, went upstairs to his room, and settled in to work.
After allowing himself a few minutes of procrastination—scouting prospective college campuses on Google Earth—Mueller navigated over to the Department of Justice’s Epstein Library portal and clicked through the page asking whether he was 18 or older (he was, just barely). Then he began poking around for ideas in the 3 million pages of Epstein files that had been added 11 days earlier.
Mueller really liked working in his bedroom, with its beanbag chair and view of people strolling and biking along one of Marin County, California’s sun-dappled waterways. Having lived his whole life in one of the wealthiest parts of America, Mueller couldn’t help thinking his area probably had some ties to Jeffrey Epstein. “I think it’s very difficult to get an immense amount of money without—this is my opinion—without doing something a little shady,” Mueller says. So he sat on his bedroom floor and spent the next five hours combing the federal database for links to the towns and cities of Marin.
He found thousands. Most of them were trivial (Epstein liked to shop online at Restoration Hardware, headquartered in nearby Corte Madera). But a few things stood out: a 2014 art gala in Sausalito that Epstein helped promote; a meeting with Woody Allen in Tiburon; and—above all—a 2013 email exchange between Epstein and a woman from a modeling agency called Mill Valley Connection. “Regarding Hannah, my Austrian model,” the woman wrote in one particularly chilling message, “we can come and see you this evening if you are interested, and in that case let me know how I can get my fees.”
Two days later, on February 12, Mueller posted his story to the Instagram feed of the Redwood Bark, his school’s student-run publication. It was a carousel-style slideshow pitched at readers across the county. “Which Marin towns were mentioned in the Epstein files?” the first panel reads. “Scroll to see how many times your town was mentioned.” Rather than quote from the most alarming document he’d found, Mueller kept his descriptions fairly general and brief: “Mill Valley was mentioned in the context of providing models to Epstein from a woman named Gisele Attias Bonnouvrier.”
More than 4,000 people liked the story. The comments filled up with praise: “This is the kind of journalism we need.” “Higher quality reporting than local outlets.” “High schoolers doing better reporting than national news.” “Didn’t think I’d be following a random CA HS newspaper in 2026 for their breaking reporting but here we are.”
As Mueller watched the numbers climb, he felt excited but also a little perplexed. “I didn’t really think I was doing groundbreaking journalism,” he says. “I was just like, this is another piece of homework that I have to do today, and I’ve just got to get it done—but also be thorough, because people are going to see it on the internet.”
About a week and a half later, Mueller was home sick with a light fever and cough when the phone rang. It was his journalism teacher, Erin Schneider, with bad news. “This person mentioned in your post is now threatening to sue the district,” she said.
On Monday, February 23, Bonnouvrier, the modeling agent, had sent an email to the principal of Redwood High School, calling Mueller’s post defamatory, demanding its immediate removal, and promising legal action if the school did not comply within 48 hours. And now the district superintendent was demanding that the Bark either redact Bonnouvrier’s name or delete the slide entirely.
The redwood bark happens to be one of the most award-winning high school newspapers in the United States. Madison Bishop—a poised, rosy-cheeked, 18-year old colleague of Mueller’s—says she was an avid Bark reader even as a kid, before her older sister served as editor in chief back in 2022. “It was just such a well-known student paper,” she says.
Bishop and Mueller both arrived on the Bark staff during a time of experimentation. Over the previous decade, Schneider and her students had pushed the Bark beyond old-school print and basic web articles, expanding into Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, LinkedIn, and a podcast. Then during the first few weeks of this past school year, Schneider says, they flipped the switch toward being “social-media first”—publishing some full stories directly to the platforms.
As the Bark’s social media manager, Bishop oversaw the transition, which she saw as a kind of power move: Social media wasn’t just where all the Bark’s students got their news, it’s where kids have the most natural authority. “It gives us a space to have a leg up from adults,” she says. “It really lets them sit down and listen and absorb what we have to say, because we are the quote-unquote professionals.”
Case in point: As soon as the Bark leaders saw the superintendent’s demands, they knew Instagram wouldn’t allow them to edit an already published slide; simply redacting Bonnouvrier’s name, in other words, was not a viable option. Another problem was that Redwood High’s principal was out of the country and unable to meet. With the pressure of a 48-hour legal threat looming over them, they would have to decide how to respond to the district on their own.
Once everyone was back at school on Tuesday, the high schoolers lawyered up during their lunch hour. Gathered around the speakerphone in Schneider’s office, Bishop and Mueller consulted an attorney with the national Student Press Law Center. When he heard the students’ problem, the lawyer laughed, Schneider recalls. “If this woman thinks she’s going to sue your school district, she’s got another thing coming,” he said. “Her name is in the Epstein files—no lawyer is going to represent her in this case.” The students also consulted Mueller’s parents—both lawyers—and another attorney, who all concluded that the Bark had done nothing wrong.
Increasingly convinced that they hadn’t defamed anyone, the Bark staffers weighed their options. After school, Mueller, Schneider, Bishop, and another Bark editor sat down on the blue couches in their newsroom for a grueling four-hour debate. Painstakingly, they double-checked every single word on Mueller’s slide, verifying it against the federal documents.
They were on the verge of deciding to leave the Instagram post alone. But after Schneider headed out for the evening, the students kept second-guessing themselves. They ended up deciding to temporarily archive Mueller’s most controversial slide until they could meet with school officials in person. “I think at the end of the day, the kids felt such pressure from the administration that they were almost looking for a reason to get out from under it,” says Schneider, who had butted heads with school officials several times that year over the Bark. (Schneider is also someone I’ve known for years; I’m a massage therapist in Marin County, and Schneider used to be an occasional client before I started working as a journalist.)
That evening, the students wrote a note advising Schneider what they wanted to communicate to the principal; they framed their takedown of Mueller’s slide as entirely their own prerogative. “We want to be clear that the removal was not in response to your request,” they wrote. “Our choice was based on our own ethical considerations and editorial standards.”
The message was puzzling to Schneider, who saw the administrators’ demand as a pretty clear example of censorship. But the Bark reporters didn’t see themselves as having given in.
Finally, that Thursday, Mueller and Bishop met in person with principal Barnaby Payne and Courtney Goode, superintendent of the Tamalpais Union High School District. Schneider came along too, but only to take notes. As she remembers it, the meeting started tense.

title: Flipper Busy Bar Review: An Expensive Focus Tool
summary: It didn’t keep my coworkers at bay, but Flipper’s expensive productivity tool did help me focus on the task at hand.
full_text:
The Busy Bar is a focus tool that blares a bright red BUSY sign. Stick it on your desk, mount it on your monitor, or put it outside your office—the device works as both a productivity timer and an indication that you are not to be interrupted. It costs $250.
It's made by Flipper Devices, the company known for the Flipper Zero—a handheld hacking tool that uses a Tamagotchi-esque Dolphin to monitor and manipulate certain radio-frequency identification (RFID) frequencies. It freaked some governments out enough that they temporarily banned the product. But the Busy Bar is a much quieter device, meant to sit on your desk or hang on your monitor to let people know you’re in the zone and not to be disturbed. It was announced in 2025, and sales kicked off in June. Flipper recently released the open source firmware on GitHub.
The device is small, roughly the size of a sunglasses case. The default screen reads BUSY, but you can swap between themes that change the message on the screen, like “KEEP OUT,” “OUT TO LUNCH,” or “LOW SOCIAL BATTERY.” The bar also works as a digital clock, and for now that’s the only other app on it.

title: Bitcoin Retreats Below $66,000 After Clarity Act and AI-Led Optimism
summary:
Bitcoin retreats from $67,000 amid broader market correction.

The post Bitcoin Retreats Below $66,000 After Clarity Act and AI-Led Optimism appeared first on Unchained.
full_text:
Bitcoin has dipped below $66,000 after climbing as much as 2.5% to trade just shy of $67,000 on Tuesday for the first time since mid-June amid optimism around the Clarity Act and AI.
The move mirrors a broader market correction as investors await Alphabet’s earnings today.
This story is an excerpt from the Unchained Daily newsletter.
Subscribe here to get these updates in your email for free
Bitcoin and the broader crypto markets had rallied on reports that the White House on Monday night signed off on ethics language for the Clarity Act, the provision that had stalled the market-structure bill for months. Stoking further optimism, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday told Fox Business that the bill is at the “1-yard line,” urging a vote before the August recess.
In the backdrop was also a broader tech rally on optimism around AI demand and looming earnings reports. Bitcoin had fallen in tandem with these stocks last Friday.
The End of Crypto Winter?
The Clarity Act optimism and the recent rally had again stoked speculation that the extended crypto market downturn is at an end.
“If [Clarity] passes, winter is over,” Bitwise investment chief Matt Hougan said on X. Amid recent developments the market is underestimating the chances of the bill passing this year, Hougan said.
Polymarket bettors most recently put the odds of the bill passing this year at 41%.
The bill has just over 10 working days left till the August recess and needs 60 votes in the Senate, which would require at least seven Democrats to cross over.

title: Movement Labs Files for Chapter 11 After Token Scandal
summary:
The company behind the Move-based layer-2 network collapsed into bankruptcy after a token-dump scandal.

The post Movement Labs Files for Chapter 11 After Token Scandal appeared first on Unchained.
full_text:
Movement Labs, the original developer behind the Movement blockchain, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy earlier this week, capping an extended period of controversy.
Movement Labs in its filings reported between $100,001 and $500,000 in assets and liabilities of up to $10 million. The company listed co-founder Rushikesh “Rushi” Manche, the Delaware Division of Revenue and Anchorage Digital among its largest creditors.
This story is an excerpt from the Unchained Daily newsletter.
Subscribe here to get these updates in your email for free
Movement Labs’ troubles began shortly after the December 2024 launch of the MOVE token.
A market-making agreement had given a little-known company Rentech control of 66 million MOVE tokens to be sold into the market one day after the token debuted, contributing to a significant price decline.
The fallout reshaped the Movement Labs. The company in May 2025 separated from Manche after internal investigations. It also transferred responsibility of Movement blockchain’s development to a separate company called Move Industries.
Move Industries last month said it would pivot away from competing with other Ethereum scaling networks and instead focus on cross-border payments, remittances, and stablecoin settlement, claiming access to licensed payment infrastructure in the U.S., Canada, and the European Union.

title: 15 家 Launchpad 角逐 Robinhood Chain：Pons 逆襲、 NOXA 登頂
summary:
Robinhood Chain 短短三週湧入 15 家 Launchpad，徹底打破生態格局。早期霸主 NOXA 跌落神壇，由 Pons 逆襲奪下流量王座。數據顯示，其單日發幣量與活躍用戶更強勢超車 Solana，Robinhood 鏈如何引爆幣圈新一輪熱錢廝殺？一文看懂最新戰況。

〈15 家 Launchpad 角逐 Robinhood Chain：Pons 逆襲、 NOXA 登頂〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
作者：Nancy，PANews
誰也沒想到，系出傳統的 Robinhood Chain 如今卻成了 MEME 發行平台的兵家必爭之地。
短短三週，這個快速成長的 Meme 新戰壕，快速吸引了 15 家 Launchpad 強勢入駐，圍繞資產發行、用戶流量和鏈上流動性的競爭正在快速升溫。
這場 Launchpad 大戰不僅推動 Robinhood Chain 生態快速擴張，也正在重塑 Meme 賽道競爭格局，甚至多個指標超過 Solana，成為新一輪鏈上流量爭奪的焦點。
Launchpad 成生態核心入口，Meme 熱度仍未退潮
Robinhood Chain 上的 Launchpad 已成為當前鏈上生態最活躍的應用場景。
Dune 數據顯示，7 月 20 日，Robinhood Chain Launchpad 相關代幣交易金額達 1.37 億美元，佔當日鏈上 DEX 總交易量的 32.7% 。同時，Launchpad 活躍位址數約 14.2 萬個，佔全鏈活躍位址總數的 51.9% 。
數據表明，Launchpad 已成為推動 Robinhood Chain 生態成長的核心入口，不僅貢獻了大量鏈上交易活動，也成為吸引用戶進入生態的重要入口。
在經歷首輪投機熱潮後，Robinhood Chain 上的 Meme 市場熱度雖較峰值有所降溫，但交易規模與用戶參與度仍保持較高水平，生態活躍度並未出現明顯回落。
從發行規模來看，隨著鏈上發行入口不斷增加，Meme 代幣數量迎來快速擴張。 Dune 數據顯示，Robinhood Chain 單日新增代幣數量已從早期的 129 個增長至峰值 4.8 萬個，隨後有所回調，但目前仍保持在超 3.4 萬個。
交易活躍度方面，Dune 數據顯示，Robinhood Chain Launchpad 單日交易額已從 6 月 30 日的約 48 萬美元成長至目前的 1.37 億美元，期間最高突破 2.6 億美元。雖然目前交易規模較高峰有所回落，但鏈上流動性已初步形成，並建立起一定市場基礎。
用戶參與度同樣保持成長趨勢。 6 月底，Robinhood Chain Launchpad 相關活躍錢包數量少於 1 萬個，隨後在 7 月快速增長，並於 7 月 11 日達到約 15.3 萬個峰值，目前仍維持在約 14.2 萬個水平。
不過，從資產品質來看，在 Robinhood Chain 鏈上發行的超 36.3 萬個代幣中，市值達到千萬美元等級的代幣僅有 3 個，包括 $CASHCAT 、 $Pons 和 $TENDIES，市值達到百萬美元等級的代幣則僅約 20 個。其中，龍頭 Meme 幣 $CASHCAT 市值已從最高 2.3 億美元已跌至 8,000 萬美元左右。
整體來看，儘管部分短期投機資金逐步退場，但鏈上用戶並未同步大幅流失，生態整體參與度仍保持活躍。
多元化平台同台競技，Pons 取代 NOXA 成為新流量中心
當下，Robinhood Chain 上的 Launchpad 生態正在多角化擴張，主要涵蓋 AI 、基礎設施、模組化發行、公平發行及 RWA 等方向。
Dune 數據顯示，6 月 30 日上線初期，Robinhood Chain 上僅有 NOXA 一家 Launchpad，而目前鏈上主要發行平台數量已成長至 15 家。
這些 Launchpad 平台各具特色，正在形成差異化競爭。例如，Pons 、 Flap 、 Bow.fun 等平台專注於模組化發行和高效能資產創建；Virtuals Protocol 、 Bankr 、 Clanker 則聚焦 AI Agent 與高級基礎設施方向；Coinbarrel V2 、 Degen Launch 、 pmav 等平台更偏向公平發行和 Degen 生態；Long.xyz 則嘗試探索代幣化股票、 RWAav 等平台更偏向公平發行和 Degen 生態；Long.xyz 則嘗試探索代幣化股票、 RWAav 與 Meme 美元資產結合的新模式。多元化的平台佈局意味著，Robinhood Chain 正在逐步建立覆蓋不同項目和使用者需求的 Launchpad 生態。
不過，在平台數量快速成長的同時，市場競爭格局也呈現出明顯的頭部效應，代幣發行量、交易規模以及用戶流量均持續向頭部平台集中。
從代幣發行量來看，生態初期 NOXA 以先發優勢佔據主要市場份額。 7 月 10 日之前，鏈上新增代幣發行幾乎全部來自 NOXA，是 Robinhood Chain 早期最主要的資產發行入口。隨著 NOXA 暫停發幣，其市佔率迅速被其他平台分食。截至 7 月 20 日數據來看，Pons 已逆襲成為目前最大的代幣發行平台，其發行數量佔整體 Launchpad 市場約 37.5%；Flap 緊隨其後，佔比約 26.6% 。
交易表現方面，NOXA 憑藉先發優勢長期佔據主導地位，交易額份額一度超過 95% 。但隨著新平台崛起，市場格局逐漸改變。 Dune 數據顯示，7 月 20 日，Pons 平台代幣交易額佔整體 Launchpad 市場約 61.7%，NOXA 佔比約 22.5%，兩者合計貢獻超過八成交易量。
用戶分佈方面，平台競爭格局變化更為直覺。 NOXA 在生態高峰時期，單日吸引超過 11.8 萬個活躍地址，佔當天 Launchpad 市佔率約 78.2% 。截至 7 月 20 日，Pons 已成為用戶規模最大的 Launchpad，活躍錢包數量佔整體活躍錢包的 51.2%；NOXA 佔比下降至約 15.5%，Flap 佔比約 9.3% 。
值得注意的是，儘管 NOXA 暫停發幣後市佔率明顯下滑，但其品牌影響力並未完全消失。目前，NOXA 域名已被 Rain.fun 收購，並作為 Robinhood Chain 上的新 Launchpad 重新上線，未來能否藉助既有品牌和用戶基礎重奪市場，仍值得持續關注。
多指標反超 Solana，Robinhood Chain 成新流量爭奪地
Robinhood Chain 正在成為 Meme 幣賽道的新興主要戰場。
相較於已形成成熟生態的 Solana Meme 市場，Robinhood Chain Launchpad 雖然發展週期較短，但在代幣發行規模和用戶參與度等指標上已經展現出較強競爭力，部分數據甚至超過 Solana 同期水準。
從每日代幣發行數量來看，Dune 數據顯示，7 月 20 日，Solana 生態 Meme 幣發行數量約 2.3 萬個，而 Robinhood Chain 同期發行數量超過 3.4 萬個，領先 Solana 近一半。
活躍用戶方面，Robinhood Chain 同樣表現更為活躍。 Dune 數據顯示，Solana Launchpad 相關活躍地址數量超過 7.9 萬個，而 Robinhood Chain 達到約 14.2 萬個，接近 Solana 的兩倍。
在收入捕獲能力方面， Dune 數據顯示，7 月 20 日，Solana Launchpad 產生收入超過 31.7 萬美元，而 Robinhood Chain 約為 27.9 萬美元。考慮到 Solana 擁有更成熟的 Meme 生態基礎，Robinhood Chain 能夠實現接近水平的收入表現，也進一步反映其 Meme 交易活動的活躍程度。
不過，儘管 Robinhood Chain 在部分指標上快速追趕 Solana，兩者的生態存在明顯差異。目前，Solana 高度依賴 Pump.fun，Robinhood Chain 則呈現多元化競爭格局。
Dune 數據顯示，7 月 20 日，Pump.fun 貢獻了 Solana 生態約 99.3% 的代幣發行量，幾乎壟斷整個賽道。同時，其代幣交易量佔 Solana Launchpad 市場約 97.7%，幾乎形成獨大的平台格局。
相較之下，Robinhood Chain 目前百花齊放，尚未形成類似 Pump.fun 的絕對壟斷平台。目前，代幣發行主要由 Pons 、 Flap 、 Clanker 、 Bow.fun 、 Bankr 以及 Virtuals 等多個 Launchpad 共同貢獻，交易流動性也主要集中於 Pons 、 NOXA 、 Flap 和 Bow.fun 等多個平台。當然，這也與 Robinhood Chain 仍處於生態早期階段有關。
而隨著生態熱度持續提升，越來越多其他鏈上的 Launchpad 開始加入競爭，包括來自 BNB Chain 、 Base 和 Solana 生態的 Flap 、 Virtuals 、 Clanker 、 Bankr 以及 Circus Trade 等平台，都嘗試在 Robinhood Chain 的新興 Meme 市場中爭奪份額。
不過，長期來看，Launchpad 生態競爭的勝負並不取決於代幣發行數量，而是平台能否提升資產品質、增強用戶留存，並形成永續發展的生態能力。

title: 《CLARITY 法案》迎重大突破？川普同意道德條款，但民主黨又拋新爭議
summary:
白宮表示川普已同意《Clarity Act》加密法案道德條款，禁止官員發行數位資產。然而由司法部執法的安排引發民主黨反彈，法案能否通過仍具變數。

〈《CLARITY 法案》迎重大突破？川普同意道德條款，但民主黨又拋新爭議〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
白宮宣稱：川普已同意 Clarity Act 道德條款
獨立媒體《Punchbowl》披露，白宮官員已跟共和黨參議員 Cynthia Lummis 跟 Bernie Moreno 會面，已就參議院正在審議的《數位資產市場清晰法案》（Clarity Act）中的道德條款達成協議。
《Clarity Act》法案已於 2025 年 7 月由眾議院通過，但因政府關門、道德爭議、代幣化與穩定幣收益等問題，在國會遭遇多次延宕。
這項初步協議是在 7 月 16 日川普與 Moreno 、 Lummis 以及白宮加密顧問 Patrick Witt 的會面中談定，但截至目前為止，法案的實質內容尚未對外公布。
一位白宮官員也對媒體《CoinDesk》表示，川普已同意史上最全面且範圍最廣的道德條款，並強調政府已竭盡所能配合民主黨的訴求。
執法權歸屬成為民主黨反彈焦點
《The Block》報導進一步揭露《Clarity Act》道德條款的部分內容，白宮加密顧問 Patrick Witt 週二在一場產業界電話會議中表示，條款規定包括總統、副總統及國會議員在內的聯邦官員，不得發行數位資產，並由司法部作為主要執法機關，而非各州檢察總長。
這項安排隨即引發民主黨不滿。民主黨參議員 Angela Alsobrooks 表示，由司法部執行道德條款是不夠嚴肅的提案，如果條文如此規定，她不會支持這項法案，但她也強調會持續努力達成讓所有人都負責任的協議。
另外兩位民主黨參議員 Kirsten Gillibrand 、 Ruben Gallego 也表示，至今仍未收到協議的完整文字內容。而川普的私人律師 Todd Blanche 目前正接受司法部長職位的任命審查，這也讓民主黨質疑，司法部是否足夠獨立來執行相關條款。
法案時程緊迫，後續仍有變數
參議院多數黨領袖 John Thune 先前已表示，《Clarity Act》法案最快可能在下週初排入院會表決議程，而 8 月 7 日參議院進入夏季休會前，被視為完成立法的重要期限。
若參議院通過，法案仍須送回眾議院進行二次表決，預計最快要等到 9 月眾議院復會後才會處理，而眾議院共和黨內部歧見也可能拖延進度。
近期，民主黨陣營內部也出現將預測市場相關政策一併納入法案討論的聲音，若成真恐讓整體協商更加複雜。
白宮方面則持續透過產業界向外界傳達訊息，強調如果參議院民主黨最終未能支持法案，責任應由民主黨承擔，因為政府自認已做出最大讓步。
比特幣價格走高，預測市場過關機率上升
雖然變數還很多，但白宮達成道德條款協議的消息傳出後，比特幣（$BTC）仍一舉突破 66,000 美元，創下七週以來新高，市場人士認為漲勢與道德協議的消息，以及川普計畫加徵 10% 國際貿易關稅的消息有關。
在預測市場 Polymarket 上，交易員們認為《Clarity Act》法案在今年完成立法的機率，已由上週五的 32%，跳升至週一的 43% 。
不過部分交易員認為，比特幣上漲的主要動能其實來自三星、 SK 海力士等記憶體廠商帶動的 AI 與半導體類股反彈，法案進展只是助漲因素之一。
（以上內容獲合作夥伴《加密城市》授權節錄及轉載，原文連結 ）

title: 比特幣金庫遭洗劫！算法穩定幣 Balance 單日閃崩 99%
summary:
演算法穩定幣「Balance Coin」因協議漏洞遭駭客利用，幣價單日暴跌逾 99%，從接近 1 美元跌至 0.0014 美元，幾乎失去所有市場價值。這起攻擊共造成協議約 91.2 萬美元資產遭竊，再次凸顯 DeFi 協議對預言機安全的高度依賴。

〈比特幣金庫遭洗劫！算法穩定幣 Balance 單日閃崩 99%〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
鏈上數據顯示，演算法穩定幣「Balance Coin」因協議漏洞遭駭客利用，幣價單日暴跌逾 99%，從接近 1 美元跌至 0.0014 美元，幾乎失去所有市場價值。這起攻擊共造成協議約 91.2 萬美元資產遭竊，再次凸顯 DeFi 協議對預言機安全的高度依賴。
Balance Coin 是一款流通規模不大的演算法穩定幣（透過協議機制維持價格，而非以法幣儲備支撐），原本設計目標是維持 1 美元價格。
然而，周三遭受攻擊後，Balance Coin 價格從前一天接近 1 美元，一度暴跌至約 0.0014 美元，跌幅超過 99%，幾乎抹去約 350 萬美元的名目市值。
雖然 Balance Coin 代幣市值蒸發數百萬美元，但駭客實際獲利約為 91.2 萬美元；遭竊資產來自 42DAO，也就是 Balance Protocol 的治理組織。
Balance Protocol 採用比特幣抵押鑄幣機制，用戶可將比特幣作為抵押品，鑄造 Balance 穩定幣；當抵押品價值低於安全門檻時，系統就會啟動清算，出售抵押資產以維持協議穩定。
區塊鏈安全公司慢霧科技（SlowMist）指出，攻擊者利用協議的預言機漏洞，人為將系統中的比特幣價格壓低至異常水準。
致命的是，Balance 的借貸合約防護機制徹底失靈，不僅未將這筆異常報價與市場真實價格區間進行比對，更未設置任何清算延遲機制，因此系統直接接受錯誤報價，導致大量原本安全的抵押倉位被誤判為應清算狀態。
這讓駭客得以在瞬間強制清算多個原本不該被清算的比特幣金庫，隨後將搜刮來的抵押品全數變現。初步估算，駭客在這次攻擊中成功套利 91.2 萬美元。
這起事件再次凸顯 DeFi 協議在預言機設計、風控機制及清算流程上的潛在風險。尤其預言機作為鏈上 DeFi 協議的重要基礎設施，一旦價格來源遭操縱，就可能引發錯誤清算、資產流失，甚至造成穩定幣脫鉤等連鎖效應。

title: Burnham says he will review early prisoner release scheme
summary: The prime minister says he cannot commit to changing the policy but wants to look at it in detail "before we go further forward".
full_text:
Burnham says he will review early prisoner release scheme
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will review the early prisoner release policy.
Speaking to reporters in Bath, he said: "I can't say that I can change the policy completely, but I will look at it in detail before we go further forward."
He acknowledged that there was "pressure on prisons places" and that a failure to invest in the prison system in the past had created "an unacceptable situation".
Tens of thousands of inmates have been let out of prison to create more space in jails since September 2024.
His comments come after the mother of police officer Andrew Harper said the potential early release of two of her son's killers felt like an "insult".
Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter but could be released early under the new Sentencing Act.
The overcrowding of the prison estate has been a problem for several years and successive government have released prisoners early in a bid to free up space.
The Sentencing Act, which was passed by Sir Keir Starmer's government earlier this year, was designed to ease pressure on prisons, and will see some offenders spend less time in prison before release.
Burnham said: "I want to assure myself that everything has been looked at before this policy proceeds, and I can give that assurance that every single part of this I will look into with the justice secretary."

title: Some food prices have fallen – but inflation expected to rise from here
summary: June's fall in inflation will be welcomed by the new prime minister but analysts warn the fall is temporary.
full_text:
Some food prices have fallen – but inflation expected to rise from here
- Published
Food prices are rising at their slowest rate in nearly two years, as the cost of some staples such as margarine and sugar have gone down.
Supermarket price wars have helped drive down prices in the year to June, the industry says, as retailers work to tempt customers with summer deals.
Inflation in the UK overall has fallen to 2.6% in the year to June, down from 2.8% in the year to May, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), driven largely by lower fuel and food prices.
June's figure will be welcomed by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his government, but analysts warn the fall is temporary, as higher energy prices in July are expected to push inflation back up.
Lower fuel costs - particularly lower diesel prices - also pushed inflation down, with prices at the pump falling for the first time since the start of the war in the Middle East.
Clothing costs fell as well due to the summer sales, with many retailers offering larger discounts than last year.
Falling food prices
Food and non-alcoholic beverage inflation fell by 0.2% month-to-month, with sugar, chocolate and confectionery seeing the largest drop in price.
Looking at inflation over the year, beef and veal price inflation eased from 9.4% in the 12 months to May to 5.1% in the year to June, while edible offal - which includes things like liver, kidneys and tongue - slowed from 9.2% to 3.4% over the same period.
Some other food items were cheaper, according to ONS data. Pizza and quiches, for example, fell by 6.7% in the year to June. Margarine dropped by 1.9% in the same period.
Food inflation often has a lag of up to 13 months due to the supply chain, so any effects from the war in Iran could still be yet to come.
Fuel prices at the pump fell in June after the US and Iran agreed to halt military operations and allow the key Strait of Hormuz to re-open.
But the recent resumption of hostilities and a new jump in crude oil prices means inflation could spike again in the coming months.
The British Retail Consortium (BRC) said lower food inflation was driven by "intense competition between supermarkets".
"If retailers are to keep prices affordable for consumers in the long run, the Government needs to take practical steps to lower the everyday cost of doing business," BRC economist Harvir Dhillon said.
"Andy Burnham has taken immediate action to ease pressure on household budgets; he must now look to do the same for businesses."
The new prime minister has pledged to make the cost of living a priority for his government, and new Chancellor John Healey said the lower rate of inflation was "news families want to hear" but "there is much more to do".
The government announced on Wednesday morning that the bus fare cap in England will be brought back down to £2 in January.
That was after Burnham announced that VAT on domestic electricity bills would be scrapped for the rest of the year from October.
Healey said: "Both these changes are a win-win. They help keep inflation down, while helping people afford the essentials."

- What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages? - Published31 minutes ago
 
Interest rate hike unlikely
The latest inflation figure is still above the Bank of England's target of 2%, but Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said a rate increase when the Bank meets next week is unlikely.
"Rate-setters may want to assess the impact of any measures announced by the new Prime Minister before deciding whether to tighten policy again," she said.
She added that rising inflation will "likely become a more notable economic headache" for Healey, "squeezing his fiscal headroom, raising borrowing costs, and increasing financial market volatility".
Yael Selfin, KPMG's chief economist, said the June figure is likely to be the lowest of the year.
Higher energy bills, brought about by a rise in Ofgem's price cap, will likely push inflation up again, she said.
"Although the impacts from the initial energy shock have so far been relatively limited, if energy prices remain high for longer, second-round effects risk feeding through into wages and more broadly across the economy."
Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at AJ Bell, said: "The markets are still only expecting a single rate hike by the end of 2026, but it's expected to hit in September, with another potentially following in February.
"It means the most generous rates are likely to edge up. If you're in the market for a new savings account, it's worth keeping your eye open for a bargain and acting fast while it lasts."
But she added: "There's miserable news for anyone in the market for a new mortgage. Mortgage rates had been falling across the board, but this week has seen them jump significantly."

title: Southampton boss Eckert charged by FA over Spygate
summary: Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert is charged by the Football Association for his role in the Spygate scandal.
full_text:
Southampton boss Eckert charged by FA over Spygate
- Published
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has been charged with misconduct by the Football Association for his role in the Spygate scandal.
Saints were kicked out of the Championship play-offs in May after admitting they spied on three clubs during the campaign.
An independent disciplinary commission ruled at the time that the espionage was authorised by Eckert and was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".
Since then the club has been the subject of an investigation by the FA, looking into who participated in the spying and assessing the culpability of those who knew it was happening.
The FA said, external Eckert "has been charged with three breaches of FA rule E3.1 in relation to misconduct between December 2025 and May 2026".
Southampton beat Middlesbrough over two legs in the play-off semi-final but, after Saints' expulsion, Boro were reinstated to the final and went on to lose to Hull City.
The English Football League (EFL) expelled Southampton from the play-offs after they admitted watching training sessions involving Oxford United and Ipswich Town, in addition to filming Middlesbrough before the semi-final.
The EFL can only take action against its member clubs but the FA can punish individuals and hand out bans.
The FA said it is "alleged that the head coach acted in an improper manner and/or brought the game into disrepute by directing and/or authorising the observation of training sessions" of these games.
Eckert has until next Tuesday to respond.
In a statement, Southampton said, external they and Eckert "acknowledge today's charges from the FA relating to a breach of rule E3.1".
The club added: "Tonda and the club will continue to co-operate fully and openly with the FA.
"Our focus remains on preparations for the 2026-27 Championship season. The club remains fully supportive of Tonda and his staff as we work towards our ambition of returning to the Premier League.
"We are unable to comment further while the process remains ongoing, but we will provide an update to supporters as soon as we are in a position to do so."
In June, Southampton owner Dragan Solak told BBC Sport he would not sack Eckert, despite the "mistake" of the head coach, and argued the club had already been punished enough.
Eckert recently told BBC Radio Solent: "It's tough to read some of the things that are out there, I've held my hand up for this judgement on something I have authorised.
"I am responsible and I apologise for bad judgement; we've be in now for a week and there comes a point to look forward and from the first day back in, there's been lots of smiles and a good energy in the place again."
Alongside last season's punishment, Southampton will start the new Championship campaign with a four-point deduction. The club's opening fixture is away at Watford on 16 August.
- Southampton expelled from play-offs for spying - Published19 May
 
- 'It hurts' - Saints boss Eckert on Spygate judgement - Published4 days ago
 
- Southampton owner will not sack head coach Eckert - Published2 June
 
From no-one to someone: the academy coach who took his chance
When Will Still was sacked by Southampton on 2 November, Saints were in 21st place - three points outside the Championship relegation zone with one win in 13 games.
That is when the club turned to Eckert, who had only arrived at St Mary's in July 2025 when he replaced a Chelsea-bound Calum McFarlane and took charge of the club's under-21 team.
He appeared perfect for that academy job.
Eckert's career had largely involved youth football, in his homeland with Bayern Munich and RB Leipzig. He had also helped the under-18s at Austrian club Red Bull Salzburg win the Uefa Youth League.
Four months after moving to Saints, he would replace Still and manage a club in one of the biggest leagues in Europe.
Eckert's only prior work in senior football came through 15 months as the number two at Barnsley, and three years as assistant boss at Italian club Genoa.
But he was well known to Johannes Spors, Southampton's sporting director, as they were at Genoa together.
So Eckert, at the age of 32 and with no previous managerial experience, stepped into Still's shoes on an interim basis which became permanent a month later.
Eckert won a hat-trick of Championship manager of the month awards - for February, March and April - as Saints not only stormed into play-offs but finished within four points of the automatic places.
Southampton (68) won more points after Eckert took charge than any other club - including champions Coventry City (67).
But just 48 hours before they played Middlesbrough in the first leg of their play-off semi-final, Southampton's world came crashing down.
William Salt - an intern analyst - was discovered observing a Middlesbrough training session, and the saga known as Spygate began.

title: OpenAI says its AI went rogue and launched 'unprecedented' cyber-attack
summary: It is one of the first publicly disclosed cyber-attacks carried out by AI without direct human involvement.
full_text:
OpenAI says its AI went rogue and launched 'unprecedented' cyber-attack
- Published
OpenAI has revealed some of its most advanced AI models went rogue and hacked a start-up after it lost control of them during a security test.
The ChatGPT-maker said its agent - an AI system which can operate alone after some human instruction – was being tested in a controlled environment, but found vulnerabilities and managed to escape.
They targeted Hugging Face, one of the world's largest hubs for sharing AI models, gaining access to some internal company systems.
OpenAI said the incident was "unprecedented", external, and it was conducting an investigation alongside Hugging Face, whose boss Clement Delangue said in a post on X it was "mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously".
"The investigation is ongoing, and we'll share more learnings from what might be the first incident of its kind," Delangue added.
Insecure sandboxes
Gina Neff, head of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the security tests - called sandboxes - are "supposed to be secure environments where you can see what the models are capable of".
"In this case, it looks like OpenAI didn't make a secure enough sandbox," she added.
Instead, the agents created their own cyber-attack against the sandbox itself, finding a vulnerability which allowed them to escape.
Once outside, the AI identified Hugging Face as a likely source of the answers they were seeking in the test, and tried to gain access.
Neil Lawrence, Professor of machine learning at Cambridge University, called it an "impressive feat", but cautioned it "falls well within the known capabilities of the current generation" of high-powered AI models.
He pointed out that OpenAI is looking to list itself on the stock market, and faces intense pressure from rival firm Anthropic, which has made headlines with its own powerful AI tool, Mythos.
"OpenAI are now playing catch-up, they are trying to demonstrate their own systems' capabilities in cyber-security."
"It shows us that OpenAI are not capable of safely deploying their own technology," he added.
In its initial disclosure of the hack on 16 July, external, Hugging Face said it was still assessing whether any customer or partner data was affected and would contact affected parties if necessary.
It said it has now closed the vulnerabilities highlighted by the incident and rebuilt the affected systems.
"Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical," it said.
"Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defence to keep pace.
"We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn."
'Sobering moment'
The incident has prompted fresh questions about the capabilities of advanced AI systems and whether existing safeguards are sufficient as the technology becomes more powerful.
Spencer Starkey, an executive at cyber-security firm SonicWall, told the BBC the incident made it clear organisations needed to "step up" their own defences and "treat cyber resilience as a core operational priority".
"The uncomfortable truth is that too many organisations are still defending at human speed while adversaries are escalating to machine speed," he said.
Meanwhile Travis Lelle, principal security engineer at cyber-security consulting firm Guidepoint Security, said the update marked a "sobering moment in cyber-security".
"This highlights a known asymmetry," he said.
"Offensive agents are unconstrained, while the best defensive tools are locked behind guardrails that cannot understand context."
But Jake Moore, global cyber-security advisor at ESET, said the announcement could also have a competitive dimension.
He argued OpenAI may be seeking to highlight its own AI capabilities as rival Anthropic attracts growing attention for its Claude Mythos model.
"It does pose the question that OpenAI are potentially chasing the marketing dream of Anthropic of late," he said.
It comes a week after Chinese AI start-up Moonshot unveiled Kimi K3 - a massive new artificial intelligence model it said could rival top US firms.

title: Modelling scout linked to Epstein found dead in Paris suburbs
summary: Daniel Siad, whose name appears in the Epstein files thousands of times, had previously denied knowledge of the threat Jeffrey Epstein posed.
full_text:
Modelling scout linked to Epstein found dead in Paris suburbs
- Published
A modelling scout linked to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein has been found dead at his home.
Daniel Siad, 69, was discovered on Monday in Colombes, a north-west suburb of Paris, the Nanterre prosecutor's office confirmed to the BBC.
"An investigation to determine the cause of death was opened on Monday evening following the discovery," the office said, adding that an autopsy will be carried out.
Siad's name appeared thousands of times in the Epstein files released by the US government. He had previously denied any knowledge of the threat that Epstein posed.
Epstein victim Anya - not her real name - previously told the BBC Siad had introduced her to Epstein.
"It was a complete set-up," she said, describing Siad as "essentially a professional trafficker".
During one e-mail to Epstein released in the files, Siad wrote in badly-spelled English: "In This busyness I feel like fisherman some time I cache quick, some time no fish".
Ahead of a BBC investigation on the subject published on 18 July, Siad's lawyer had said he was not available for comment.
In a recent CNN interview, Siad said he did not know the women were being abused by Epstein: "I trusted him, I believed this guy is a professional person."
Siad himself was the subject of several complaints in France, including allegations of rape, with the first filed in February. He denied wrongdoing in multiple recent media interviews, telling BFMTV in May: "I have never raped anyone in my life."
A former model who had given a deposition to police in June as part of the investigation into Siad told the BBC his death meant information he may have had about Epstein was now lost.
"An important link in the chain has just vanished into thin air, without there even having been a chance to recover the information Daniel Siad might have possessed—given that he was never questioned," she said.
"Too much time has been lost... and it is yet another way for the leads to go cold. I hope we won't have to wait another seven years to see his home searched, even though I think it is already too late."
Anne-Claire Le Jeune, part of a group of lawyers from NGO Innocence en Danger which pushed for the start of an investigation into Epstein in Paris in 2019, said victims had been deprived of justice.
"My clients found the strength to break a particularly heavy silence, given Daniel Siad's ties to Jeffrey Epstein," she said. "They faced every stage of the proceedings with remarkable courage."
"It is deeply regrettable that the slow pace of the investigation resulted in his death before he could be questioned or taken into police custody, thereby depriving the victims of a crucial step in their pursuit of truth and justice."

title: YouTube star MrBeast marries Thea Booysen
summary: The world's biggest YouTuber said he had finally found his "Mrs Beast".
full_text:
YouTube star MrBeast marries Thea Booysen
- Published
YouTube star MrBeast has tied the knot with his fiancee Thea Booysen.
The pair married on Richard Branson's private Necker Island in the British Virgin Islands, according to US outlets.
The 28-year-old US content creator announced he had "found MrsBeast" in a joint Instagram post, external, which featured images of them posing in white on their big day.
MrBeast, real name Jimmy Donaldson, is the biggest YouTuber in the world with more than 500m subscribers.
Donaldson popped the question to Booysen on Christmas Day 2024 while they wore matching MrBeast-branded festive jumpers.
He previously told US outlet People magazine that despite being known for huge online stunts, he wanted a "really private and intimate" proposal and small wedding.
In photos shared by the couple, Booysen can be seen wearing a floor length lace wedding dress with a floral pattern, while Donaldson opted for a white tuxedo.
Booysen also had several outfit changes throughout the day, including a white mini dress with a sparkly bodice and feathered skirt for cutting the cake, and an off-the-shoulder satin look for later in the evening.
MrBeast described it as "the best day of my life" in the post.
Donaldson has built a massive following over the years by creating viral videos and staging stunts for his YouTube channel.
These have snowballed into huge high-stakes challenges where he gives away large sums of money to strangers.
He also helped create the Prime Video reality competition series, Beast Games, which was inspired by the hit Netflix show Squid Game.
It follows contestants as they play a series of games in the hope of winning a $5m (£3.7m) prize pot.
Booysen, originally from South Africa, also has her own channel on the site, TheaBeasty, with nearly 140,000 subscribers.
The 28-year-old also streams games on Twitch and is a published author.
Being the most successful YouTuber has not come without controversy for Donaldson.
In April, MrBeast's media company, Beast Industries, was sued by a former employee over claims of sexual harassment and workplace gender bias.
He has also faced legal action by contestants in the Beast Games on how they were treated, as well as claims his viral giveaways and competitions are staged and pre-planned.

title: From singing in a bar to performing as an alien in new Supergirl film
summary: Winnie Ama couldn't believe her luck when she had the chance to sing her original song in the new Supergirl movie - but there was a catch.
full_text:
How a singer's chance encounter led to an alien experience in Hollywood
- Published
"Would you like to be in my film?"
It's a question any singer songwriter dreams of being asked by a big movie director, and when the question was put to Winnie Ama after performing in a bar one night, she couldn't believe her luck.
But there was a catch.
As part of her role in the new Supergirl movie, her original song What Are We needed to be translated into an alien language.
Two weeks after the Belfast singer's chance encounter with the film's director, she and her pianist were invited for an official audition.
"I had never acted before, so I was sweating quite a lot, but we made it, and we got the part in the room," Winnie said.
"We went for fittings straight away, and it went from there."
She was cast to play a singing alien in the new Supergirl film, which was released last month.
'I've always wanted to be an alien'
Winnie is well used to the spotlight - from performing in London bars to outdoor music festivals - but singing in an alien language brought a whole new world of challenges.
Her character performs her original song in an alien bar in space, when Supergirl visits the planet of Bilquis.
What Are We is the first song Winnie released as a solo artist in 2020, and an alien language specialist was hired to help her translate it into the Bilquis language.
"We went through each word and each syllable to make sure that the pronunciation was perfect for Bilquis," she said.
"He told me about the structure and the origins of the language that he created, which was so cool, because he's the guy who created other alien languages like [Star Trek's] Klingon.
"Being a Bilquis alien was so much fun, I've always wanted to be an alien."
During production she would have to wake up at 4am to travel to the film set at Leavesden in time to get her Bilquis costume on.
"The hair, the make up, everything was applied by hand and it took about four hours - and at the end of the day they would scrub me down."
What Are We fits well into the narrative of the film because the song "is about conflict, and there is a lot of conflict in the film", Winnie said.
"Supergirl is navigating a lot of conflict and trauma - and in the song I'm really questioning what it's like whenever you start to question a relationship, whether it's a friend or someone you live with where you just fundamentally disagree and there's some elephants in the room that you have to navigate."
The DC Studios Supergirl film, directed by Craig Gillespie and starring Milly Alcock, follows a reluctant superhero on a quest to save her dog, Krypto, teaming up with a bounty hunter named Lobo, played by Jason Momoa.
"We've had so many different versions of Superman and not that many about Supergirl," Winnie said.
"I think this film is really important because it's not your traditional superhero, she's like a real person with real emotions.
"I think it's quite ahead of its time."

title: 'Lip King' banned twice before woman's BBL death
summary: Alice Webb's family say she would have never had a BBL if she knew about previous bans.
full_text:
'Lip King' banned twice before woman's BBL death
- Published
A cosmetic practitioner arrested after the death of a mother-of-five had been banned from carrying out liquid Brazilian Butt Lift (BBL) procedures in two other parts of England, the BBC has learned.
Jordan Parke, known as the "Lip King", faced enforcement action in Dudley and Greater Manchester before treating Alice Webb in Gloucester in 2024.
Webb's former partner, Ben Kingscote, said the case highlighted gaps in regulation and called for a national system to prevent practitioners operating elsewhere.
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said ministers would consult on tougher measures covering high-risk cosmetic procedures, including liquid BBLs.
A BBL is a non-surgical cosmetic procedure in which dermal fillers are injected into the buttocks to alter their size or shape.
More from Gloucestershire
- 'I was abused after meeting man on dating app' - Published6 hours ago
 
- Man crushed to death after safety fence removed - Published19 hours ago
 
- Time Team star to headline history festival - Published15 hours ago
 
Kingscote said Webb, from Wotton-under-Edge in Gloucestershire, would not have undergone the procedure had she known about the previous enforcement action.
"If Alice had known about these prohibition orders she wouldn't have had it done," he said.
"Her kids were everything to her. She adored her kids. She wouldn't have done something that would have jeopardised that."
Gloucestershire Police had been investigating the death of Webb, 33, who died in hospital after becoming unwell following the treatment.
In October, a BBC investigation reported Parke, 34, had been arrested on suspicion of manslaughter in connection with her death but had not been charged.
Parke, who had appeared on television shows to talk about his work, died in February in an unrelated incident which is believed to have happened after he underwent a cosmetic procedure.
Gloucestershire's senior coroner said Webb's inquest would likely take place in front of a jury in the autumn.
The BBC has now learned concerns about Parke's practice were first raised in Dudley in 2019.
Dudley Council issued a prohibition order in 2023 preventing him from carrying out liquid BBL procedures in the area.
A second prohibition order was issued in Salford in February 2024.
Kingscote said the local restrictions did not prevent Parke from continuing to work elsewhere and he should have been banned nationally.
"The agencies in Dudley and Salford issued him with prohibition orders.
"He was prohibited from doing this in those parts of the country but that didn't stop him from moving down here to Gloucester.
"If a procedure is dangerous in one part of the country it's dangerous in all parts of the country."
Kingscote, who is the father of Alice's eldest daughter, said the family's loss continued to be felt every day.
"The hardest bit by far was telling the kids," he said. "You think about it all the time. It never goes away. But Alice should be here to see the achievements they're making. She would be so proud.
"My daughter's mum should still be here - Alice should still be here."
He said he and Alice's daughter Delsie, 17, had wanted to make sure she felt present at her prom so ensured she was in the photographs.
Kingscote believes the case demonstrates the need for a national approach to regulating high-risk cosmetic procedures.
Patient safety organisation Save Face said it had repeatedly warned ministers that stronger regulation was needed.
Co-founder Ashton Collins said: "Since 2023 we have been campaigning for a national law that would make it illegal for anyone other than a GMC-registered plastic surgeon to carry out liquid BBLs and other high-risk body contouring procedures.
"Our proposal is simple: a clear, nationwide offence that applies to all providers, not piecemeal local action."
She added: "We warned government repeatedly that without such legislation someone would die.
"In 2024 that prediction became a reality when Alice Webb tragically and needlessly lost her life."
BBL warning
Save Face has warned of an increase in serious complications linked to BBL procedures, including infections, sepsis and abscesses requiring hospital treatment.
The organisation has called for the procedure to be banned outside regulated medical settings.
Last year, the government announced plans, external that would mean only qualified healthcare professionals could carry out high-risk procedures such as non-surgical BBLs.
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "We are taking action to crack down on cosmetic cowboys and root out dangerous practices."

title: Glasgow School of Art cannot afford to restore fire-hit Mackintosh building
summary: The art school previously insisted it was committed to a faithful reinstatement of the building.
full_text:
Glasgow School of Art cannot afford to restore fire-hit Mackintosh building
- Published
Glasgow School of Art says it cannot fully restore the city's iconic Mackintosh Building to its former state without additional financial support.
The art school previously insisted it was committed to a faithful reinstatement of the building, which was designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh but wrecked by two fires in 2014 and 2018.
However it now says "financial clarity", provided by an insurance settlement regarding the 2018 blaze, has shown it "cannot take forward the faithful reinstatement on its own."
Instead it suggests the building has potential to be an anchor for a "creative and cultural production innovation district".
But this claim that has attracted scorn from figures in the art world.
The GSA's new report into restoration plans says several factors - including construction inflation, market volatility and economic pressure - have made the reinstatement of the Mackintosh far more expensive than predicted in a previous report, published in 2021.
The report states fully restoring the Mackintosh is therefore "dependent on external funding sources that are uncertain", and cites a "significant funding gap" needing to be resolved.
It believes the total cost of restoring the Mackintosh would be £265m.
Ann Priest, the chair of the school's board of governors, told BBC Scotland News: "What we are doing is what is affordable to us.
"The school cannot possibly, on its own, rebuild this whole building. It would take us away from financial sustainability.
"We are still hoping to go towards a full, faithful reinstatement. It's not going to be an exact replica, due to changes in construction and building [standards]."
She said the school would now look for "visionary individuals" who could bring "serious investment" to the project, as well as governments and local authorities.
The GSA will now remove external scaffolding about the building, saying this will improve the building's presentation and visibility, as well as helping stabilise the site.
Priest added that this will be the first step in "the reinstatement for whatever this building is going to become" and called the new proposals a landmark move for the long-term future of the site.
She said: "We have looked at the economic case, what does Glasgow need, what do our students need and what will benefit the school, the building and the creative and cultural industries."
The painter and writer Lachlan Goudie told BBC Scotland News the possibility of the art school not being restored to its former self was a disgrace.
He said he feared the more time passes from the fires, the higher chance people will start to forget the building.
Goudie said: "This reeks of a lack of transparency, which has been very common over the past eight years. The fact it has taken that long to get to a point where we know nothing much, beyond the GSA don't have enough money to rebuild it, is shameful.
"It is a national disgrace what has happened here. Nothing less than an authentic recreation of what Mackintosh left Glasgow and the world will do.
"We had the World Cup recently, and we should be as proud of the building as we are of the national football team. The Scottish government need to be saying this is vital to our national character - we had architectural crown jewels left to us."
When asked by BBC Scotland if she would consider the Mackintosh being taken outwith the board of governors and perhaps be passed to a trust if they fail to secure further investment, Priest said she was confident more funding would be achieved.
The first fire ripped through the Art School building on 23 May 2014.
Four years later an even more devastating fire broke out - this time occurring near the end of a £35m restoration project.
Since then GSA said about £26m of funding has gone towards work on restoring the historic building, which was first completed in 1910.
However work stalled after a dispute with insurers, resulting in a long-running arbitration claim. GSA now say this was settled to its satisfaction last month.
But it declined to reveal any details of what was awarded in the case, only saying the total came short of the number needed to carry out a full restoration of the building.
The report lists several cultural organisations based near Sauchiehall Street, including Scottish Opera, the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland and the National Theatre of Scotland.
It proposes formal recognition of this so-called cluster, saying it would be "a creative and culture-led innovation district would bring significant opportunities" for Glasgow as a whole, with the Mackintosh serving as a "cultural anchor" to the plan.
The Art School says it will seek to begin discussions immediately with the city, government, stakeholders and potential partners over this proposal.
However the mention of this cluster, which was not previously discussed in prior papers, has raised scepticism from some.
Prof Alan Dunlop, who studied architecture at the GSA, has previously criticised GSA management's handling of the two fires and ran for chair of the board in 2022.
He told BBC Scotland News the new plans feature "so many if's and but's".
He added: "This seems to me to be a dilution of responsibility, and worse, a distinct failure to focus on their prime task of delivering a replacement for the Mackintosh building, rather than enabling some centre for creative activity.
"There's no legitimate pathway described at all for the delivery for the 'faithful reinstatement' of the building."
Prof Dunlop says he fears the building is gone forever, as it would be impossible to rebuild to modern health and safety standards.
He also queried how the £265m figure had been reached by the GSA.
Priest told BBC Scotland the figure had been calculated through work with various leading architects.

title: Police station opens at Hitler's birthplace in bid to rid site of Nazi link
summary: The opening follows years of controversy about what to do with the 17th-Century former inn, where the Nazi dictator was born.
full_text:
Police station opens at Hitler's birthplace in bid to rid site of Nazi link
- Published
Austria has opened a police station in the house where Adolf Hitler was born, in the town of Braunau am Inn.
It follows years of controversy about what to do with the 17th-Century former inn, where Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler was born in April 1889.
The building has now been substantially refurbished and its facade changed, but it has been a huge headache for Austrian authorities, who want to prevent it from becoming a site of neo-Nazi pilgrimage.
Hitler only lived in Salzburger Vorstadt 15 for a few weeks, before his family moved to another address in Braunau. They left the town for good when he was three years old.
Hitler returned briefly to Braunau in 1938, on his way to Vienna, after he annexed Austria to Nazi Germany.
For decades, the interior ministry rented the building from its former owner, a local woman called Gerlinde Pommer. It paid her a generous rent, in an attempt to prevent the house being used as a site for extreme right-wing tourism.
The building was used for many years by a local charity as a day centre and workshop for people with special needs. But it was forced to move out in 2011, when Pommer blocked renovations.
She also repeatedly refused to sell the property to the government.
The house remained empty for several years, while the authorities and Pommer argued over terms.
In 2016, Austria's parliament passed a law allowing the government to seize the house from Mrs Pommer. It paid her compensation of €812,000 (£690,000). She later took the government to court, saying the sum was too low, but lost her case.
The interior minister at the time, Wolfgang Sobotka, said the building should be torn down and a new one erected in its place. It was an echo of an earlier offer by a Russian MP who said he wanted to buy the house and blow it up.
But there was a storm of criticism, with many saying that destroying the house would be tantamount to denying Austria's Nazi past.
In 2019, the government announced plans to turn it into a police station, and initiated a EU-wide competition for architects to submit designs.
Millions of euros were spent refurbishing the old yellow building, which now looks very different from before.
Not everyone is happy with the decision to open a police station there, saying it sends the wrong signal.
Some had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, confronting the Nazi past. Others, like local historian Florian Kotanko, say they would have liked to have seen the Lebenshilfe charity return.
"But even this charity organisation did not want to come back because they thought they would be used as a fig leaf for a political discussion, and so the government had to decide in another way," Kotanko told the BBC.
There is no sign on the house about its history and the building features security cameras to record the activities of any potential neo-Nazi pilgrims.
All that links it to Hitler is a stone on the street outside, which was erected in 1989.
It says: "Never again Fascism; In memory of millions of dead."
The stone comes from the nearby former concentration camp at Mauthausen.
Hitler's name does not appear. However, Florian Kotanko believes the site's history will never go away even if fewer neo-Nazis pay a visit.
"You have to deal with it, and so we all try to deal with it in an open and correct way. It's not a matter of being proud, but it's a matter of dealing with the fact."
